questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass $M$ moves along a horizontal $x$ axis from $x=0$ to $x=L$. The coefficient of kinetic friction varies as a function of $x$ as $\mu_k(x)=\mu_0-\alpha x$, where $\mu_0$, $\alpha$ are constants of appropriate dimensions, so that $\mu_k(L)=0$. The total work done by the frictional force during the motion is $n\mu_0 MgL$, where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity. The value of $n$ is :
questions.solution:
Given the coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu_k(x) = \mu_0 - \alpha x$

At $x = L$, $\mu_k(L) = 0 \Rightarrow \mu_0 - \alpha L = 0 \Rightarrow \alpha = \dfrac{\mu_0}{L}$

The frictional force acting on the particle is $f_k = \mu_k(x) Mg = \left(\mu_0 - \dfrac{\mu_0}{L}x\right)Mg$

The magnitude of work done by the frictional force is given by:

$|W| = \int_{0}^{L} f_k dx$

$|W| = \int_{0}^{L} \left(\mu_0 - \dfrac{\mu_0}{L}x\right) Mg dx$

$|W| = Mg \left[ \mu_0 x - \dfrac{\mu_0 x^2}{2L} \right]_{0}^{L}$

$|W| = Mg \left( \mu_0 L - \dfrac{\mu_0 L^2}{2L} \right) = \dfrac{1}{2} \mu_0 MgL$

Comparing this with $n \mu_0 MgL$, we get $n = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{2}$

questions.q: An object falls from a height of 10 m above the ground. After striking the ground it loses $50 \%$ of its kinetic energy. The height upto which the object can rebounce from the ground is:
questions.solution:
K.E. just before striking the ground $K_1=m g h_1=m g(10)$
K.E. just after striking the ground $=K_1-\frac{50}{100} K_1=\frac{50}{100} K_1=\frac{K_1}{2}=K_2$
Now, $K_2=m g h_2$
$\Rightarrow \frac{K_1}{2}=m g h_2$
$\Rightarrow \frac{m g(10)}{2}=m g h_2 \Rightarrow h_2=5 \mathrm{~m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The power of a crane, which lifts a mass of $1000$ kg to a height of $20$ m in $10$ s is :
($g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$)
questions.solution:
Given $m = 1000$ kg, $h = 20$ m, $t = 10$ s, $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$.

Work done by the crane is $W = mgh$.

$W = 1000 \times 9.8 \times 20 = 196000$ J.

Power is the rate of doing work, $P = \dfrac{W}{t}$.

$P = \dfrac{196000}{10} = 19600$ W.

$P = 19.6$ kW.

Answer: $19.6$ kW

questions.q: An electric lift with a maximum load of $2000kg$ (lift $+$ passengers) is moving up with a constant speed of $1 . 5{ms}^{- 1}$. The frictional force opposing the motion is $3000N$. The minimum power delivered by the motor to the lift in watts is : $\left(g = 10{ms}^{- 2}\right)$
questions.solution:
Since the speed is constant the motor has to give equal and opposite upward force.

$∴ F = 3000N + 2000 \times 10$ $= 23000N$

$P = FV = 23000 \times 1 . 5$ $= 34500W$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The potential energy of a long spring when stretched by $2cm$ is $U$. If the spring is stretched by $8cm$, potential energy stored in it will be:
questions.solution:
Potential energy stored in spring is given by,

$U = \dfrac{1}{2}K{x}^{2} .$

First case:

$U = \dfrac{1}{2}K{\left(2 \times {10}^{- 2}\right)}^{2} . . . Eq\left(1\right)$

Second case:

${U}^{'} = \dfrac{1}{2}K{\left(8 \times {10}^{- 2}\right)}^{2} . . . Eq\left(2\right)$

From both equations, we get

$\dfrac{U}{{U}^{'}} = \dfrac{1}{16} ⇒ {U}^{'} = 16U$

Change in potential energy of water per second $= 15 \times g \times 60$

$= 9000J{s}^{- 1}$

Energy remaining per second after loss $= 90 %$ of $9000J{s}^{- 1}$

$= \left(\dfrac{90}{100}\right) \times 9000$

$= 8100J{s}^{- 1}$

$= 8 . 1kW$

questions.q: A body initially at rest and sliding along a frictionless track from a height $h$ (as shown in the figure) just completes a vertical circle of diameter $AB = D$. The height $h$ is equal to,
questions.solution:
To just complete a vertical circle, speed at A should be

${v}_{A} = \sqrt{5gR}$

Using energy conservation

$mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}_{A}^{2}$

$h = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{{v}_{A}^{2}}{g} = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{5g}{g}\dfrac{D}{2}$ $\left(R = \dfrac{D}{2}\right)$

$h = \dfrac{5D}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A force $F = 20 + 10y$ acts on a particle in $y$-direction where $F$ is in Newton and $y$ is in meter. Work done by this force to move the particle from $y = 0$ to $y = 1m$ is
questions.solution:
Work done is calculated by taking the dot product between the force and the displacement.

$W = ∫ F \cdot dy$
$= \mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}20\text{d}y + \mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}10ydy$
$= {\left[20y\right]}_{0}^{1} + 5{\left[{y}^{2}\right]}_{0}^{1}$
$= 20 + 5 = 25J$

$\overset{\to}{S} = \overset{\to}{r}2 - \overset{\to}{r}1 = \left(4\overset{^}{j} + 3\overset{^}{k}\right) - \left(- 2\overset{^}{i} + 5\overset{^}{j}\right)$

$= 2\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} + 3\overset{^}{k}$

$\overset{\to}{F} = 4\overset{^}{i} + 3\overset{^}{j}$

$W = \overset{\to}{F} . \overset{\to}{s} = 8 - 3 = 5J$

questions.q: A body of mass $1kg$ begins to move from rest under the action of a time dependent force $\overset{\to}{F} = \left(2t\overset{^}{i} + 3{t}^{2}\overset{^}{j}\right)N$, where $\overset{^}{i}$and $\overset{^}{j}$ are unit vectors along x and y axis. What power will be developed by the force at the time t?
questions.solution:
$\overset{\to}{a} = 2t\overset{^}{i} + 3{t}^{2}\overset{^}{j}$

$\overset{\to}{\text{V}} = \dfrac{{2t}^{2}}{2} \overset{^}{i} + \dfrac{3}{3} {t}^{3} \overset{^}{j}$

$\overset{\to}{F} = 2t\overset{^}{i} + 3{t}^{2}\overset{^}{j}$

$P = \overset{\to}{F} . \overset{\to}{V} = 2{t}^{3} + 3{t}^{5}$

kinetic energy of the ball on reaching ground

${v}_{0} = \sqrt{2gh} = 20\text{m}{\text{s}}^{- 1}$

questions.q: A particle of mass $m$ is driven by a machine that delivers a constant power $k$ watts. If the particle starts from rest the force on the particle at time $t$ is:
questions.solution:
\(\begin{aligned}
& F v=\text{ constant }=\mathrm{k} \\
& \mathrm{So}, \\
& \frac{\mathrm{mdv}}{\mathrm{dt}} \mathrm{v}=\mathrm{k} \\
\Rightarrow & \int \mathrm{vdv}=\int \frac{\mathrm{k}}{\mathrm{m}} \mathrm{dt} \\
\Rightarrow & \frac{\mathrm{v}^2}{2}=\frac{\mathrm{k}}{\mathrm{m}} \mathrm{t} \\
\Rightarrow & \mathrm{v}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{k}}{\mathrm{m}} \mathrm{t}}
\end{aligned}\)
Now,
\(\begin{aligned}
& F=\frac{\mathrm{mdv}}{\mathrm{dt}} \\
& =\mathrm{m} \sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{k}}{\mathrm{m}}} \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{t}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \\
& =\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{mk}}{2}} \mathrm{t}^{-\frac{1}{2}}
\end{aligned}\)

questions.q: A block of mass $10kg$, moving in $x$ direction with a constant speed of $10m{s}^{- 1}$ , is subjected to a retarding force $F = \left[( 0 .1 )x\right]J{m}^{- 1}$ during its travel from $x = 20m$ to $30m$ . Its final kinetic energy will be:
questions.solution:
$m = 10kg, u = 10m{s}^{- 1}$

Final KE will be given by

$K{E}_{f} = K{E}_{i} + W$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}m{u}^{2} + \mathop{∫}_{20}^{30}\left(- 0 .1 x\right)dx$

$= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 100 + \left(- 0.1\right){\left[\dfrac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right]}_{20}^{30}$

$= 500 + \dfrac{\left(- 0.1\right)}{2}\left(900 - 400\right)$

$K{E}_{f} = 500 + \dfrac{\left(- 0.1\right)500}{2}$$= 475J$

questions.q: One coolie takes 1 minute to raise a suitcase through a height of $2 \mathrm{~m}$ but the second coolie takes $30 \mathrm{~s}$ to raise the same suitcase to the same height. The power two coolies are in the ratio
questions.solution:
We know that
$$
\text{ Power }=\frac{\text{ Work done }}{\text{ Time }}
$$

Work done $=m g h$ is same in both the case
$$
\therefore \frac{\mathrm{P}_1}{\mathrm{P}_2}=\frac{f_2}{f_1}=\frac{30 \mathrm{sec}}{1 \mathrm{~min}}=\frac{1}{2}
$$

questions.q: A body of mass $1 \mathrm{~kg}$ is thrown upwards with a velocity $20 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$. It momentarily comes to rest after attaining a height of $18 \mathrm{~m}$. How much energy is lost due to air friction ? $\left(\mathrm{g}=10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}\right)$
questions.solution:
Key Idea The energy lost due to air friction is equal to difference of initial kinetic energy and final potential energy.
Initially body posses only kinetic energy and after attaining a height the kinetic energy is zero.
Therefore, loss of energy $=\mathrm{KE}-\mathrm{PE} \begin{aligned}$& =$\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv}^$2-$\mathrm{mgh}$\\
& =$\frac{1}{2} \times$1 $\times$400-1 $\times$18 $\times$10 \\
& =200-180=20 $\mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A body of mass $3 \mathrm{~kg}$ is under a constant force which causes a displacement $s$ in metres in it, given by the relation $s=\frac{1}{3} t^2$, where $t$ is in seconds. Work done by the force in 2 seconds is:
questions.solution:
It is given that:
$s=\frac{t^2}{3}$
Differentiating w.r.t. $t$ we have
$U=\frac{d s}{d t}=\frac{2 t}{3}$
Again differentiating w.r.t. $t$ we have
$a=\frac{d^2 s}{d t^2}=\frac{2}{3}$
Now $\mathrm{W}=\int \mathrm{F} d s=\int \mathrm{mads} \begin{aligned}
& =\int m \times \frac{2}{3} \times \frac{2 t}{3} d t \\
& =\frac{4}{9} m \int t d t \\
W & =\frac{4}{9} m \times\left[\frac{t^2}{2}\right]_0^2 \\
& =\frac{4}{9} \times 3 \times 2=\frac{8}{3} \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}$

It is given that:

Differentiating w.r.t. $t$ we have

Again differentiating w.r.t. $t$ we have
$a=\frac{d^2 s}{d t^2}=\frac{2}{3}$
Now $\mathrm{W}=\int \mathrm{F} d s=\int \mathrm{mads} \begin{aligned}
& =\int m \times \frac{2}{3} \times \frac{2 t}{3} d t \\
& =\frac{4}{9} m \int t d t \\

questions.q: A particle is moved along a path $AB - BC - CD - DE - EF - FA,$ as shown in figure, in presence of a force $\overset{\to}{F} = \left(\alphay\overset{^}{i} + 2\alphax\overset{^}{j}\right)N,$ where $x$ and $y$ are in meter and $\alpha = - 1N / {m}^{- 1} .$ The work done on the particle by this force $\overset{\to}{F}$ will be ____ Joule.
questions.solution:
$dw = \overset{\to}{F} ⋅ d\overset{\to}{r}$
$dw = aydx + 2axdy$
Now, total work done in whole path is given by,
$W = {W}_{AB} + {W}_{BC} + {W}_{CD} + {W}_{DE} + {W}_{EF} + {W}_{FA}$
$A \to B, y = 1, dy = 0, {W}_{A \to B} = ∫ \alphaydx = \alpha ⋅ 1\mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}dx = \alpha$
$B \to C, x = 1, dx = 0, {W}_{B \to C} = 2\alpha ⋅ 1\mathop{∫}_{1}^{0.5}dy = - 2\alpha\left(0.5\right) = - \alpha$
$C \to D, y = 0.5, dy = 0, {W}_{C \to D} = \mathop{∫}_{1}^{0.5}\alphaydx =\alpha ⋅ \dfrac{1}{2}\mathop{∫}_{1}^{0.5}dx = - \dfrac{\alpha}{4}$
$D \to E, x = 0.5, dx = 0, {W}_{D \to E} = 2\alpha ∫ xdy = 2\alpha ⋅ \dfrac{1}{2}\mathop{∫}_{1}^{0.5}dy = - \dfrac{\alpha}{2}$
$E \to F, y = 0, dy = 0, {W}_{EF} = 0$
$F \to A, x = 0, dx = 0, {W}_{E \to A} = 0$
$∴ W = \alpha - \alpha - \dfrac{\alpha}{4} - \dfrac{\alpha}{2} = - \dfrac{3\alpha}{4}$
Given $\alpha = - 1 ⇒ W = + \dfrac{3}{4}J = 0.75J$

questions.q: A tennis ball is dropped on a horizontal smooth surface. It bounces back to its original position after hitting the surface. The force on the ball during the collision is proportional to the length of compression of the ball. Which one of the following sketches describes the variation of its kinetic energy $K$ with $t$time most appropriately? The figures are only illustrative and not to the scale.
questions.solution:
When ball of mass $' m '$ dropped from height and strikes to ground.It's kinetic energy is converting into elastic potential energy due to compression.

So after time $' t '$ its final velocity,

$v = u + at$

$u$ is initial velocity of ball, $a$ is acceleration of ball and $t$ is time.

$⇒ v = 0 + \left(- g\right)t$

$v = - gt$

Negative sign shows downward direction.

Now kinetic energy of ball,

$K . E . = \dfrac{1}{2}{mv}^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}m{\left(- gt\right)}^{2}$

$⇒ K . E . = \dfrac{1}{2}{mg}^{2}{t}^{2}$

$⇒ K . E . ∝ {t}^{2}$

So, it is upward parabola. But after complete compression, $K . E .$ becomes zero, then ball will reshape again. Kinetic energy will not be constant.

questions.q: A potential is given by $V ( x ) = k ( x + a{)}^{2} / 2$ for $x < 0$ and $V ( x ) = k ( x - a{)}^{2} / 2$ for $x > 0$. The schematic variation of oscillation period $T$ for a particle performing periodic motion in this potential as a function of its energy $E$ is
questions.solution:
Given, potential function for the oscillating particle is

$V\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}\dfrac{k ( x + a{)}^{2}}{2}, & x < 0 \\ \dfrac{k ( x - a{)}^{2}}{2}, & x > 0\end{cases}\right$

So, potential energy of the particle (mass
$m$) is

$U\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}\dfrac{km ( x + a{)}^{2}}{2}, & x < 0 \\ \dfrac{km ( x - a{)}^{2}}{2}, & x < 0\end{cases}\right$

$\dfrac{dU}{dx} = \left\{\begin{cases}km ( x + a ) , & x < 0 \\ km ( x - a ) , & x > 0\end{cases}\right$

If $\dfrac{dU}{dx} = 0,$ when $x = \pm a$

Now, $\dfrac{{d}^{2}U}{d{x}^{2}} = km > 0$

So, particle is in unstable equilibrium at $x = \pm a$

Hence, particle is unbounded for $- a > x$ and $x > a$

In region, $- a \le x \le a$, time period of particle reduces from a maximum.
So, correct graph is (b)..

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Two identical trains move in opposite senses in equatorial plane with same speeds relative to the earth's surface. They have equal magnitude of normal reaction.
Reason (R): The trains have different centripetal accelerations due to different speeds.
options: Both $A$ and $R$ are true and $R$ is a correct explanation for $A$
Both $A$ and $R$ are true but $R$ is not a correct explanation for $A$
questions.solution:
The train which is moving along the direction of rotation of earth that is west to east, will require less centripetal force compared to train moving in opposite direction.

Since the centripetal force is more on the train which move along the direction of rotation of earth therefore the normal reaction acting on the train will be more.

The centripetal force is the function of relative angular velocity of earth and train, therefore the train will have different acceleration because of relative angular velocity between train and earth not due to different speed.

Statement I A block of mass $m$ starts moving on a rough horizontal surface with a velocity $v$. It stops due to friction between the block and the surface after moving through a certain distance. The surface is now tilted to an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the horizontal and the same block is made to go up on the surface with the same initial velocity $v$. The decrease in the mechanical energy in the second situation is smaller than that in the first situation.
Statement II The coefficient of friction between the block and the surface decreases with the increase in the angle of inclination.
options: Statement I is true, Statement II is true; Statement II is a correct explanation for Statement I
Statement I is true, Statement II is true; Statement II is NOT a correct explanation for Statement I

questions.solution:

$\begin{aligned}
& \Delta U_2=\frac{1}{2} m v^2-m g h \\
& \Delta U_2 < \Delta U_1
\end{aligned} \therefore \quad \Delta U_2 < \Delta U_1$
or Statement $\mathrm{I}$ is correct.
In Statement II Coefficient of friction will not change or this Statement is wrong.
$\therefore$ Option (c) is correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Consider the following statements $A$ and $B$ identify the correct answer given below :
(A) A body initially at rest is acted upon by a constant force. The rate of change of its kinetic energy varies linearly with time
(B) When a body is at rest, it must be in equilibrium.
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2} m v^2=\frac{1}{2} m(a t)^2=\frac{1}{2} m a^2 t^2$
Rate of change of KE,
$\frac{d K}{d t}=\frac{d}{d t}\left(\frac{1}{2} m a^2 t^2\right)=m a^2 t$
$\therefore \quad \frac{d K}{d t} \propto t$
So, statement $A$ is correct.
When the body is at rest, then it may be or may not be in equilibrium, so statement $B$ is wrong.

questions.q:
Statement (I) : The slope of kinetic energy-displacement curve of a body in motion will be directly proportional to its acceleration.

Statement (II) : From a height of $15 \mathrm{~m}$ a ball is projected vertically upwards with a velocity of $30 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. If the ball rises to the same height after hitting the ground, the loss of its energy on hitting the ground is $30 \%$.
Statement (III) : The velocity acquired by a body of mass ' $m$ ' after travelling a fixed distance from rest under the action of a constant force is directly proportional to mass ' $\mathrm{m}$ '. 
Which of the following is correct?
options: Statements I, II, III are true
Statements I, III are true, but statement II is false
Statement I is true, but statements II and III are false
Statements I, II are true, but statement III is false
questions.solution:
We have
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{K} . \mathrm{E}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mV}^2 \\
& \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{dx}}(\mathrm{K} . \mathrm{E})=\frac{1}{2} \times \mathrm{m} \times 2 \mathrm{~V} \frac{\mathrm{dV}}{\mathrm{dx}}
\end{aligned}$
Slope of $($ K.E $-\mathrm{x})$ curve $=\mathrm{ma} \propto \mathrm{a}$
So, (I) is correct
When ball just strike the ground, then
$\mathrm{V}=\sqrt{30^2+2 \times 10 \times 15}=\sqrt{1200} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$
If ball reaches the same height after striking the ground then, velocity after collision $=30 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \begin{aligned}
& \text{ So, } \Delta \mathrm{E}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}(1200-900) \\
& =\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m} \times 300 \\
& \frac{\Delta \mathrm{E}}{\mathrm{E}} \times 100=\frac{\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m} \times 300}{\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m} \times 1200} \times 100=25 \%
\end{aligned}$
So, (II) is incorrect.
Now, equation of motion are independent of mass. So velocity will not depend on mass. So (III) is incorrect.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Assertion : At any instant the magnitude of rate of change of potential energy of the projectile of mass 1 kg is numerically equal to magnitude of a v (where, a is acceleration due to gravity and v is velocity at that instant).
Reason : The graph representing power delivered by the gravitational force acting on the projectile with time will be straight line with negative slope.
options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
If Assertion is true but Reason is false
If Assertion is false but Reason is true
questions.solution:
\($\begin{array}{l} 
& \text{Assertion } \frac{d U}{d t} =\frac{d}{d t}(m g h)=m g \frac{d}{d t}\left(u_y t-\frac{1}{2} g t^2\right) \\
& =m g\left(u_y-g t\right)=m g v_y \\
& \therefore \left|\frac{d v}{d t}\right| =m g\left|v_y\right|
\end{array}$
For
$\begin{aligned}
m & =1 \mathrm{ kg} \\
\left|\frac{d U}{d t} \right\rvert\, & =g\left(u_y-g t\right)  \quad \ldots (ii) \\
\mathrm{a} \cdot \mathrm{v} & =(-g \hat{\mathrm{j}}) \cdot\left[u_x \hat{\mathrm{i}}+\left(u_y-g t\right) \hat{\mathrm{j}}\right] \\
& =g\left(u_y-g t\right) \quad \ldots (ii)
\end{aligned}\)
From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we can see that two magnitudes are equal.
Reason \(P=\mathrm{F} \cdot \mathrm{v}=(-m g \hat{\mathrm{i}}) \cdot\left[v_x \hat{\mathrm{i}}+\left(u_y-g t\right) \hat{\mathrm{j}}\right]\)
\(=-m g u_y+m g^2 t\)
So, \(P\) versus t graph has the positive slope.$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Assertion: Spring force is a conservative force.
Reason : Potential energy is defined only for conservative forces.
options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
If Assertion is true but Reason is false
If Assertion is false but Reason is true
questions.solution:
Spring force follows Hooke's law \(F=-k x\).
Work done by spring depends only on initial and final positions, not the path \(\rightarrow\) so it is conservative.
For conservative forces, we can define a potential energy function (\(U=\frac{1}{2} k x^2\)).
Hence, spring force is conservative because potential energy is defined only for conservative forces.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Identify the correct statements from the following:

(A) Work done by a man in lifting a bucket out of a well by means of a rope tied to the bucket is negative

(B) Work done by gravitational force in lifting a bucket out of a well by a rope tied to the bucket is negative

(C) Work done by friction on a body sliding down an inclined plane is positive

(D) Work done by an applied force on a body moving on a rough horizontal plane with uniform velocity is zero

(E) Work done by the air resistance on an oscillating pendulum is negative

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Work done is given by, $W = Fscos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the force and the displacement.

case(A): Direction of force and displacement both are in the same direction and hence work done will be positive. Hence, wrong.

case(B): Direction of force and displacement both are in the opposite direction and hence work done will be negative. Hence, correct.

case(C): Direction of force and displacement both are in the opposite direction and hence work done will be negative. Hence, wrong.

case(D): Direction of force and displacement both are in the same direction and hence work done will be positive. Hence, wrong.

case(E): Direction of force and displacement both are in the opposite direction and hence work done will be negative. Hence, correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A particle of unit mass is moving along the x-axis under the influence of a force and its total energy is conserved. Four possible forms of the potential energy of the particle are given in column I (a and ${U}_{0}$ are constants). Match the potential energies in column I to the corresponding statement(s) in column II.
  Column I   Column II
A. ${U}_{1}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2}{\left[1 - {\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right)}^{2}\right]}^{2}$ P. The force acting on the particle is zero at $x = a$
B. ${U}_{2}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2}{\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right)}^{2}$ Q. The force acting on the particle is zero at $x = 0$ .
C. ${U}_{3}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2}{\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right)}^{2}exp ⁡ \left[- {\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right)}^{2}\right]$ R. The force acting on the particle is zero at $x = - a$
D. ${U}_{4}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2}\left[\dfrac{x}{a} - \dfrac{1}{3}{\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right)}^{3}\right]$ S. The particle experiences an attractive force towards $x = 0$ in the region $\left|x\right| < a$
    T. The particle with total energy $\dfrac{{U}_{0}}{4}$ can oscillate about the point $x = - a$
questions.solution:
${U}_{1}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2}{\left[1 - \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}\right]}^{2}$
$F = - \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2}2\left[1 - \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}\right]\left[- \dfrac{2x}{{a}^{2}}\right]$
$= \dfrac{2{U}_{0}}{{a}^{4}}\left[{a}^{2} - {x}^{2}\right]x$
$F = \dfrac{2{U}_{0}}{{a}^{4}}x\left(a - x\right)\left(a + x\right)$
$F = 0$ , at $x = 0, a, - a$
$\left\begin{array}{ll}x = - a, U = 0, \\ x = 0, U = \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2}\end{array}\right\} ⇒$ Oscillate when total ME is less then $\dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2}$
$A \to P, Q, R, T$
B- ${U}_{0}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2}{\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right)}^{2}$
$F = - \dfrac{{U}_{0}x}{{a}^{2}}$
$F = 0, x = 0$
$B \to Q, S$
C- ${U}_{3}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2}\left[{\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right)}^{2}exp ⁡ \left(- \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}\right)\right]$
$F = - \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2}\left[\dfrac{2x}{{a}^{2}}exp ⁡ \left(- \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}\right) + \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}exp ⁡ \left(- \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}\right)\left(- \dfrac{2x}{{a}^{2}}\right)\right]$
$= - \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2}\dfrac{2x}{{a}^{4}}exp ⁡ \left(- \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}\right)\left[{a}^{2} - {x}^{2}\right]$
$= \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{{a}^{4}}{e}^{\dfrac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}}\left[x\left(x + a\right)\left(x - a\right)\right]$
$x = 0, x = - a, x = + a, F = 0$
$x = 0, U = 0$ even function hence minima
$C \to P, Q, R, S$
D- ${U}_{4}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2}\left[\dfrac{x}{a} - \dfrac{{x}^{3}}{3{a}^{3}}\right]$
$F = - \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{a}\left[\dfrac{1}{a} - \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{3}}\right] = \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2{a}^{3}}\left[{x}^{2} - {a}^{2}\right]$
$x = + a, x = - a, F = 0$
$x = - a, U = - \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{3}, x = + a, U = + \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{3}$
Hence oscillate about $x = - a$ if $T . M . E < \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{3}$
$D \to P, R, T$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
In the List-I below, four different paths of a particle are given as functions of time. In these functions, $\alphaand\beta$ are positive constants of appropriate dimensions and $\alpha \ne \beta$ . In each case, the force acting on the particle is either zero or conservative. In List-II, five physical quantities of the particle are mentioned: $\overset{\to}{p}$ is the linear momentum, $\overset{\to}{L}$ is the angular momentum about the origin, K is the kinetic energy, U is the potential energy and E is the total energy. Match each path in List-I with those quantities in List-II, which are conserved for that path.
  LIST -I   LIST-II
A) $\overset{\to}{r}\left(t\right) = \alphat\overset{^}{i} + \beta\overset{^}{j}$ P) $\overset{\to}{p}$
B) $\overset{\to}{r}\left(t\right) = \alphacos ⁡ \omegat\overset{^}{i} + \betasin ⁡ \omegat\overset{^}{j}$ Q) $\overset{\to}{L}$
C) $\overset{\to}{r}\left(t\right) = \alphacos ⁡ \omegat\overset{^}{i} + sin ⁡ \omegat\overset{^}{j}$ R) $K$
D) $\overset{\to}{r}\left(t\right) = \alphat\overset{^}{i} + \dfrac{\beta}{2}{t}^{2}\overset{^}{j}$ S) $U$
    T) $E$
questions.solution:
$( i )$ $\overset{\to}{r}\left(t\right) = \alphat\overset{^}{i} + \betat\overset{^}{j}$
$\overset{\to}{v} = \dfrac{d\overset{\to}{r}\left(t\right)}{dt} = \alpha\overset{^}{i} + \beta\overset{^}{j}$ {constant}
$\overset{\to}{a} = \dfrac{\overset{\to}{dv}}{dt} = 0$
$\overset{\to}{P} = m\overset{\to}{v}$ (remain constant)
$k = \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}$ {remain constant}
$\overset{\to}{F} = - \left[\dfrac{∂ U}{∂ x}\overset{^}{i} + \dfrac{∂ U}{∂ y}\overset{^}{i}\right] = 0$
$⇒ U \to$ constant
$E = K + U$
$\dfrac{d\overset{\to}{L}}{dt} = - \overset{\to}{τ} = \overset{\to}{r} \times \overset{\to}{F} = 0$
$\overset{\to}{L} =$ constant
$( ii )$ $\overset{\to}{r} = \alphacos ⁡ \left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{i} + \betasin ⁡ \left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{j}$
$\overset{\to}{v} = \dfrac{d\overset{\to}{r}}{dt} = - \alpha\omegasin ⁡ \left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{i} + \beta\omegacos ⁡ \left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{j}$
$\overset{\to}{a} = \dfrac{d\overset{\to}{v}}{dt} = - \alpha{\omega}^{2}cos ⁡ \left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{i} + \beta\omegasin ⁡ ⁡ \left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{j}$
$= - {\omega}^{2}\left[\alphacos ⁡ \left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{i} + \betasin ⁡ \left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{j}\right]$
$\overset{\to}{a} = = - \alpha{\omega}^{2}$
$\overset{\to}{τ} = \overset{\to}{r} \times \overset{\to}{F} = 0\left\{\overset{\to}{r}and\overset{\to}{F}areparallel\right\}$
$∆ U = - ∫ F . dr + {∫}_{0}^{r}m{\omega}^{2} . r . dr$
$∆ U = m{\omega}^{2}\left[\dfrac{{r}^{2}}{2}\right]$
$U ∝ {r}^{2}$
$r = \sqrt{{\alpha}^{2}\cos^{2} ⁡ \left(\omegat\right) + {\beta}^{2}\sin^{2} ⁡ \left(\omegat\right)}$
R is a function of time (t)
U depends on r hence it will change with time
Total energy remain constant because force is central
$( iii )$ $\overset{\to}{r}\left(t\right) = \alpha\left(cos ⁡ \omegat\overset{^}{i} + sin ⁡ \left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{j}\right)$
$\overset{\to}{v}\left(t\right) = \dfrac{d\overset{\to}{r}\left(t\right)}{dt} = \alpha\left[- \omegasin ⁡ \left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{i} + \omegacos ⁡ \left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{j}\right]$
$\left|\overset{\to}{v}\right| = \alpha\omega$ (Speed remains constant)
$\overset{\to}{a}\left(t\right) = \dfrac{d\overset{\to}{v}\left(t\right)}{dt} = \alpha\left[- {\omega}^{2}cos ⁡ \left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{i} + {\omega}^{2}sin ⁡ \left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{j}\right]$
$= - \alpha{\omega}^{2}\left[cos ⁡ \left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{i} + sin ⁡ \left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{j}\right]$

questions.q:
A body is moved along a straight line by a machine delivering a power proportional to time (\(P \propto t\)). Then, match the following. \(
Column IColumn II
(A) Velocity is proportional to(p) t
(B) Displacement is proportional to(q) t^2
(C) Work done is proportional to(r) t^3
\)
questions.solution:
\(P \propto t\)
\(W=\int P d t=\int \alpha t d t \quad \text{ or } \quad W \propto t^2\)
Since, work done is equal to change is KE
Hence, \(\quad v^2 \propto t^2\) or \(v \propto t\)
Further, \(\quad v=\frac{d s}{d t}\)
\(\therefore \quad \frac{d s}{d t} \propto t \quad \text{ or } \quad d s \propto t d t\)
or \(s \propto t^2\) (by integration)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a ball dropped from a height $h$ loses $75\%$ of its kinetic energy on striking the ground, it will rebound to a height of $h/4$.
Reason (R): The rebound velocity of the ball is directly proportional to the square root of its remaining kinetic energy.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.
questions.solution:
Assertion is true: The kinetic energy just before striking the ground is $E = mgh$. If $75\%$ of the kinetic energy is lost, the remaining kinetic energy is $25\%$ of $E$, which is $E/4$. The rebound height $h'$ is given by $mgh' = E/4 = mgh/4$, so $h' = h/4$.

Reason is true: Kinetic energy is $K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, which means $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2K}{m}}$. Thus, the rebound velocity is directly proportional to the square root of the remaining kinetic energy.

However, the Reason does not correctly explain the Assertion. The correct explanation for the Assertion is that the rebound height is directly proportional to the remaining kinetic energy ($h' \propto K$), not the velocity. Therefore, both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation.

Answer: Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The power delivered by a machine varies with time. A graph of power (in $\text{kW}$) on the y-axis versus time (in $\text{s}$) on the x-axis forms a triangle with vertices at $(0\text{ s}, 0\text{ kW})$, $(10\text{ s}, 5\text{ kW})$, and $(20\text{ s}, 0\text{ kW})$. The total work done by the machine during this $20\text{ s}$ interval is
questions.solution:
The total work done is equal to the area under the power-time graph.

The graph is a triangle with base $= 20\text{ s}$ and height $= 5\text{ kW}$.

Convert the peak power to watts: $5\text{ kW} = 5000\text{ W}$.

$\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$

$W = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 20\text{ s} \times 5000\text{ W}$

$W = 50000\text{ J} = 50\text{ kJ}$

Answer: $50\text{ kJ}$

questions.solution:
The work done by the variable force is calculated by integrating the force with respect to position:

$W = \int_{0}^{4} F \, dx = \int_{0}^{4} 6x \, dx$

$W = \left[ 3x^2 \right]_{0}^{4} = 3(4)^2 - 0 = 48\text{ J}$

According to the work-energy theorem, the net work done on the block is equal to its change in kinetic energy:

$W = \Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \dfrac{1}{2}mu^2$

Since the block starts from rest, $u = 0$:

$48 = \dfrac{1}{2}(6)v^2 - 0$

$48 = 3v^2$

$v^2 = 16 \Rightarrow v = 4\text{ m/s}$

Answer: $4\text{ m/s}$

questions.q: Two particles A and B are subjected to forces. The ratio of the magnitudes of forces acting on A and B is $1:2$, and the ratio of their speeds is $4:1$. The angle between the force and velocity vectors for particle A is $60^\circ$, while for particle B it is $30^\circ$. The ratio of the instantaneous power delivered to particle A to that of particle B is:
questions.solution:
Instantaneous power is given by $P = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v} = Fv \cos \theta$.

For particle A: $P_A = F_A v_A \cos 60^\circ$
For particle B: $P_B = F_B v_B \cos 30^\circ$

Taking the ratio of their powers:
$\dfrac{P_A}{P_B} = \left(\dfrac{F_A}{F_B}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{v_A}{v_B}\right) \times \dfrac{\cos 60^\circ}{\cos 30^\circ}$

Substituting the given values:
$\dfrac{P_A}{P_B} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{4}{1}\right) \times \dfrac{1/2}{\sqrt{3}/2}$

$\dfrac{P_A}{P_B} = 2 \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$

The ratio is $2:\sqrt{3}$.

Answer: $2:\sqrt{3}$

questions.q: A pump draws water from a lower reservoir and delivers it to a nozzle located $15\text{ m}$ above the reservoir. The water is ejected from the nozzle at a speed of $20\text{ m s}^{-1}$ with a constant mass flow rate of $10\text{ kg s}^{-1}$. What is the total mechanical power delivered by the pump to the water? (Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
The pump does work to both lift the water against gravity and impart kinetic energy to it.

Rate of change of potential energy (Power for lifting):
$P_{\text{PE}} = \dfrac{dm}{dt} g h = 10 \times 10 \times 15 = 1500\text{ W} = 1.5\text{ kW}$

Rate of change of kinetic energy (Power for ejection):
$P_{\text{KE}} = \dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{dm}{dt} v^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times (20)^2 = 5 \times 400 = 2000\text{ W} = 2.0\text{ kW}$

Total mechanical power delivered by the pump:
$P_{\text{total}} = P_{\text{PE}} + P_{\text{KE}} = 1.5\text{ kW} + 2.0\text{ kW} = 3.5\text{ kW}$

Answer: $3.5\text{ kW}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electric motor consumes an input power of $10\text{ kW}$ and operates with an efficiency of $80\%$. It is used to pull a block of mass $400\text{ kg}$ horizontally across a rough surface at a constant speed. If the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the surface is $0.5$, what is the speed of the block? (Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
The useful mechanical power output of the motor is a fraction of the input electrical power, determined by its efficiency.

$P_{\text{out}} = \eta \times P_{\text{in}}$
$P_{\text{out}} = \dfrac{80}{100} \times 10000\text{ W} = 8000\text{ W}$

The frictional force acting on the block on a horizontal surface is given by $f = \mu_k mg$.
$f = 0.5 \times 400 \times 10 = 2000\text{ N}$

Since the block moves at a constant speed, the pulling force $F$ exerted by the motor must exactly balance the frictional force.
$F = f = 2000\text{ N}$

Using the relation between power, force, and velocity ($P = F \times v$):
$8000 = 2000 \times v$
$v = \dfrac{8000}{2000} = 4\text{ m s}^{-1}$

Answer: $4\text{ m s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a particle of mass $m$ is released from rest at $x=0$ in a region where the one-dimensional force acting on it is given by $F(x) = F_0 - kx$ (where $F_0$ and $k$ are positive constants), its maximum kinetic energy during the subsequent motion is $\dfrac{F_0^2}{2k}$.

Reason (R): The kinetic energy of the particle is maximum at the position where its displacement from the origin is maximum.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
The kinetic energy of the particle is maximum when its velocity is maximum, which occurs when its acceleration (and thus the net force) becomes zero.

Setting $F(x) = 0$:
$F_0 - kx = 0 \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{F_0}{k}$

The maximum kinetic energy is equal to the work done by the force up to this position. Using the work-energy theorem:
$W = \int_{0}^{\dfrac{F_0}{k}} (F_0 - kx) dx$
$W = \left[ F_0 x - \dfrac{k x^2}{2} \right]_{0}^{\dfrac{F_0}{k}}$
$W = F_0 \left( \dfrac{F_0}{k} \right) - \dfrac{k}{2} \left( \dfrac{F_0}{k} \right)^2$
$W = \dfrac{F_0^2}{k} - \dfrac{F_0^2}{2k} = \dfrac{F_0^2}{2k}$

Thus, the maximum kinetic energy is $\dfrac{F_0^2}{2k}$, making the Assertion (A) true.

At the position of maximum displacement, the particle momentarily comes to rest, meaning its kinetic energy is zero, not maximum. Therefore, the Reason (R) is false.

Answer: (A) is true but (R) is false

questions.q:
A car of mass $2000$ kg moves up a rough inclined plane at a constant speed of $10$ m/s. The incline makes an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal such that $\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{20}$. If the constant frictional force acting on the car is $500$ N, the power output of the car's engine is :
($g = 10$ m/s$^2$)
questions.solution:
Since the car moves at a constant speed, its acceleration is zero, meaning the net force acting on it is zero.

The driving force $F$ provided by the engine must balance both the downward component of gravity along the incline and the opposing frictional force $f$.

$F = mg \sin\theta + f$

$F = \left(2000 \times 10 \times \dfrac{1}{20}\right) + 500$

$F = 1000 + 500 = 1500$ N.

The power output of the engine is given by the product of the driving force and the velocity.

$P = F \times v$

$P = 1500 \times 10 = 15000$ W.

$P = 15$ kW.

Answer: $15$ kW

$60000 = m \times 10 \times 10$

$m = 600\text{ kg}$

questions.q: A particle moves in the $x$-$y$ plane such that its position vector at any time $t$ is given by $\vec{r} = (2t^2 \hat{i} + 5t \hat{j})$ m. If it is acted upon by a constant force $\vec{F} = (3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j})$ N, the instantaneous power delivered by the force at $t = 1$ s is:
questions.solution:
The position vector of the particle is $\vec{r} = (2t^2 \hat{i} + 5t \hat{j})$ m.

The velocity vector $\vec{v}$ is the rate of change of the position vector:
$\vec{v} = \dfrac{d\vec{r}}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt}(2t^2 \hat{i} + 5t \hat{j}) = (4t \hat{i} + 5 \hat{j})$ m/s

At $t = 1$ s, the velocity is:
$\vec{v} = (4(1) \hat{i} + 5 \hat{j}) = (4\hat{i} + 5\hat{j})$ m/s

The instantaneous power $P$ is the dot product of force and velocity:
$P = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v} = (3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}) \cdot (4\hat{i} + 5\hat{j})$
$P = (3 \times 4) + (4 \times 5) = 12 + 20 = 32$ W.

Taking the dot product with the position vector instead of velocity would incorrectly give 26 W, and multiplying the magnitudes of the vectors would give $5\sqrt{41}$ W.

Answer: 32 W

questions.solution:

Velocity of the particle is given by:

At $t = 2 \text{ s}$, the instantaneous velocity is:
$v = 2(2) + 1 = 5 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The instantaneous power is given by $P = Fv$.
Substituting the given values:
$50 = F \times 5$
$F = 10 \text{ N}$

Answer: $10 \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass $2 \text{ kg}$ moves along the positive $x$-axis under the action of a position-dependent force $F$. The force increases linearly from $0$ to $10 \text{ N}$ between $x = 0$ and $x = 2 \text{ m}$, remains constant at $10 \text{ N}$ from $x = 2 \text{ m}$ to $x = 4 \text{ m}$, and then remains constant at $-5 \text{ N}$ from $x = 4 \text{ m}$ to $x = 8 \text{ m}$. If the initial velocity of the particle at $x = 0$ is $4 \text{ m/s}$, the kinetic energy of the particle at $x = 8 \text{ m}$ is
questions.solution:
According to the work-energy theorem, the net work done by the force equals the change in kinetic energy of the particle: $W_{\text{net}} = K_f - K_i$.

The initial kinetic energy is:
$K_i = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times (4)^2 = 16 \text{ J}$

The work done is the algebraic sum of the areas under the force-position graph:
Work from $x = 0$ to $x = 2 \text{ m}$ (area of triangle) = $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 10 = 10 \text{ J}$
Work from $x = 2$ to $x = 4 \text{ m}$ (area of rectangle) = $2 \times 10 = 20 \text{ J}$
Work from $x = 4$ to $x = 8 \text{ m}$ (area of rectangle) = $4 \times (-5) = -20 \text{ J}$

Total work done $W_{\text{net}} = 10 + 20 - 20 = 10 \text{ J}$.

Using the work-energy theorem:
$K_f - 16 = 10$
$K_f = 26 \text{ J}$

Answer: 26 J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An object of mass $m$ starts from rest and is driven by an engine that delivers a constant power $P$. The velocity $v$ of the object varies with time $t$ as:
questions.solution:
The power $P$ delivered by the engine is constant.

Power is given by the product of force and velocity:
$P = Fv$

According to Newton's second law, $F = m \dfrac{dv}{dt}$, so:
$P = \left(m \dfrac{dv}{dt}\right) v$
$v dv = \dfrac{P}{m} dt$

Integrating both sides from $t = 0$ (where $v = 0$) to time $t$:
$\int_0^v v dv = \int_0^t \dfrac{P}{m} dt$
$\dfrac{v^2}{2} = \dfrac{P}{m} t$
$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2P}{m}} t^{1/2}$

Since $P$ and $m$ are constants, the velocity is proportional to $t^{1/2}$ ($v \propto t^{1/2}$).

Assuming constant force instead of constant power would incorrectly lead to $v \propto t$.

Answer: $v \propto t^{1/2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $m$ is projected with an initial velocity $v_0$ on a rough horizontal surface. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the surface increases linearly with the distance $x$ from the starting point as $\mu_k = bx$, where $b$ is a positive constant. The distance $D$ at which the block comes to rest is :
questions.solution:
According to the Work-Energy Theorem, the net work done on the block equals its change in kinetic energy: $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$

The frictional force acting on the block at a distance $x$ is $f_k = \mu_k mg = bxmg$.

The work done by friction as the block moves from $x=0$ to $x=D$ is:

$W_f = \int_{0}^{D} (-f_k) dx = -\int_{0}^{D} bxmg dx = -bmg \left[ \dfrac{x^2}{2} \right]_{0}^{D} = -\dfrac{1}{2}bmgD^2$

The change in kinetic energy is $\Delta K = K_f - K_i = 0 - \dfrac{1}{2}mv_0^2$

Equating the two:

$-\dfrac{1}{2}bmgD^2 = -\dfrac{1}{2}mv_0^2$

$bmgD^2 = mv_0^2$

$D^2 = \dfrac{v_0^2}{bg}$

$D = \dfrac{v_0}{\sqrt{bg}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{v_0}{\sqrt{bg}}$
questions.question: A block of mass $m$ is projected with an initial velocity $v_0$ on a rough horizontal surface. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the surface increases linearly with the distance $x$ from the starting point as $\mu_k = bx$, where $b$ is a positive constant. The distance $D$ at which the block comes to rest is :
questions.explanation:
According to the Work-Energy Theorem, the net work done on the block equals its change in kinetic energy: $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$

The frictional force acting on the block at a distance $x$ is $f_k = \mu_k mg = bxmg$.

The work done by friction as the block moves from $x=0$ to $x=D$ is:

$W_f = \int_{0}^{D} (-f_k) dx = -\int_{0}^{D} bxmg dx = -bmg \left[ \dfrac{x^2}{2} \right]_{0}^{D} = -\dfrac{1}{2}bmgD^2$

The change in kinetic energy is $\Delta K = K_f - K_i = 0 - \dfrac{1}{2}mv_0^2$

Equating the two:

$-\dfrac{1}{2}bmgD^2 = -\dfrac{1}{2}mv_0^2$

$bmgD^2 = mv_0^2$

$D^2 = \dfrac{v_0^2}{bg}$

$D = \dfrac{v_0}{\sqrt{bg}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{v_0}{\sqrt{bg}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle's kinetic energy increases from $8\text{ J}$ to $20\text{ J}$ as it undergoes a displacement $\Delta\vec{r} = (3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j})\text{ m}$. The constant force acting on the particle is given by $\vec{F} = (2\hat{i} + F_y\hat{j})\text{ N}$. The value of the unknown force component $F_y$ is
questions.solution:
According to the work-energy theorem, the net work done on a particle equals its change in kinetic energy:
$W = \Delta K = K_f - K_i$

Given $K_i = 8\text{ J}$ and $K_f = 20\text{ J}$:
$W = 20 - 8 = 12\text{ J}$

The work done by the constant force is given by the dot product of force and displacement:
$W = \vec{F} \cdot \Delta\vec{r}$
$W = (2\hat{i} + F_y\hat{j}) \cdot (3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j})$
$W = (2)(3) + (F_y)(-2) = 6 - 2F_y$

Equating the two expressions for work done:
$6 - 2F_y = 12$
$-2F_y = 6$
$F_y = -3\text{ N}$

Answer: $-3\text{ N}$

questions.q: A particle of mass $2 \mathrm{~kg}$ initially at rest is acted upon by a constant force $\vec{F} = (4\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}) \mathrm{~N}$. The instantaneous power delivered by the force at $t = 3 \mathrm{~s}$ is:
questions.solution:
From Newton's second law, the acceleration of the particle is:

$\vec{a} = \dfrac{\vec{F}}{m} = \dfrac{4\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}}{2} = (2\hat{i} + \hat{j}) \mathrm{~m~s}^{-2}$

Since the particle starts from rest ($\vec{u} = 0$), its velocity at time $t = 3 \mathrm{~s}$ is:

$\vec{v} = \vec{u} + \vec{a}t = 0 + (2\hat{i} + \hat{j})(3) = (6\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}) \mathrm{~m~s}^{-1}$

The instantaneous power delivered by the force is the dot product of force and velocity:

$P = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v}$

$P = (4\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}) \cdot (6\hat{i} + 3\hat{j})$

$P = (4)(6) + (2)(3) = 24 + 6 = 30 \mathrm{~W}$

Answer: $30 \mathrm{~W}$

questions.q: The variation of force $F$ acting on a particle with its position $x$ is represented by a straight line graph. The force increases linearly from $10\text{ N}$ at $x = 0$ to $30\text{ N}$ at $x = 4\text{ m}$. The work done by the force in moving the particle from $x = 0$ to $x = 4\text{ m}$ is
questions.solution:
The work done by a variable force is equal to the area under the force-position ($F-x$) graph.

The given graph is a straight line from $(0, 10)$ to $(4, 30)$, which forms a trapezium with the $x$-axis.

The parallel sides of the trapezium are $F_1 = 10\text{ N}$ and $F_2 = 30\text{ N}$, and the perpendicular distance between them is $x = 4\text{ m}$.

$W = \text{Area of trapezium} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times (F_1 + F_2) \times x$

$W = \dfrac{1}{2} \times (10 + 30) \times 4$

$W = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 40 \times 4 = 80\text{ J}$

Answer: $80\text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $10\text{ kg}$ is pulled up a rough inclined plane of angle $37^\circ$ at a constant speed of $2\text{ m s}^{-1}$. If the power delivered by the pulling force is $160\text{ W}$, what is the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline? (Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$, $\sin 37^\circ = 0.6$, $\cos 37^\circ = 0.8$)
questions.solution:
The power delivered by the pulling force is given by $P = F_{\text{pull}} v$.

$160 = F_{\text{pull}} \times 2 \Rightarrow F_{\text{pull}} = 80\text{ N}$

Since the block moves up the incline at a constant speed, the net force on it is zero. The pulling force must balance both the component of gravity along the incline and the kinetic friction force ($f_k$).

$F_{\text{pull}} = mg \sin\theta + f_k$

$80 = (10)(10)(0.6) + f_k$

$80 = 60 + f_k \Rightarrow f_k = 20\text{ N}$

The normal force exerted by the incline on the block is:
$N = mg \cos\theta = (10)(10)(0.8) = 80\text{ N}$

The coefficient of kinetic friction is:
$\mu_k = \dfrac{f_k}{N} = \dfrac{20}{80} = 0.25$

Using $mg \sin\theta$ instead of $mg \cos\theta$ for the normal force leads to the incorrect value of $0.33$. Ignoring the gravity component entirely leads to $1.0$.

Answer: $0.25$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): If water is pumped out of a hose pipe of constant cross-sectional area, the mechanical power required is proportional to the square of the ejection velocity.

Reason (R): The force required to eject the water stream is proportional to the square of its ejection velocity.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
For a hose pipe of constant cross-sectional area $A$, the mass of water ejected per unit time is $\dfrac{dm}{dt} = \rho A v$, where $\rho$ is the density of water and $v$ is the ejection velocity.

The force required to eject the water is equal to the rate of change of momentum of the water stream:
$F = v \dfrac{dm}{dt} = v(\rho A v) = \rho A v^2$

Thus, $F \propto v^2$. Therefore, the Reason (R) is true.

The mechanical power required by the pump is the product of force and velocity:
$P = Fv = (\rho A v^2)v = \rho A v^3$

Thus, $P \propto v^3$. The Assertion (A) states that power is proportional to the square of the velocity, which is false.

Hence, (A) is false but (R) is true.

Answer: (A) is false but (R) is true

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $m$ is pulled along a horizontal rough surface with a constant coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu$. A downward vertical force that varies with position as $F_y = cx$ (where $c$ is a positive constant) is applied to the block as it moves from $x=0$ to $x=d$. The magnitude of the total work done by the frictional force on the block is :
questions.solution:
The normal force acting on the block at position $x$ is given by $N = mg + F_y = mg + cx$.

The frictional force acting on the block is $f_k = \mu N = \mu(mg + cx)$.

The magnitude of work done by the frictional force is the integral of this force from $x=0$ to $x=d$:

$|W| = \int_{0}^{d} f_k dx$

$|W| = \int_{0}^{d} \mu (mg + cx) dx$

$|W| = \mu \left[ mgx + \dfrac{cx^2}{2} \right]_{0}^{d}$

$|W| = \mu \left( mgd + \dfrac{cd^2}{2} \right)$

Answer: $\mu \left(mgd + \dfrac{cd^2}{2}\right)$

questions.q: An electric motor rated at $2\text{ kW}$ operates continuously for $30\text{ minutes}$. The total electrical energy consumed by the motor is
questions.solution:
The electrical energy consumed is given by $E = P \times t$

Given power $P = 2\text{ kW} = 2000\text{ W}$

Time $t = 30\text{ minutes} = 30 \times 60\text{ s} = 1800\text{ s}$

Therefore, $E = 2000 \times 1800 = 3600000\text{ J} = 3.6 \times 10^{6}\text{ J}$

Answer: $3.6 \times 10^{6}\text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a variable force given by $F = \dfrac{a}{x^2}$, where $F$ is in newtons, $x$ is in meters, and $a$ is an unknown constant. If the work done by this force in moving the particle from $x = 1\text{ m}$ to $x = 2\text{ m}$ is $10\text{ J}$, what is the value of the constant $a$ in SI units?
questions.solution:
The work done by a variable one-dimensional force is given by the definite integral of the force with respect to position.

$W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F \, dx$

Substitute the given force function and limits:

$W = \int_{1}^{2} \dfrac{a}{x^2} \, dx$

Integrate using the power rule ($\int x^{-2} dx = -x^{-1}$):

$W = a \left[ -\dfrac{1}{x} \right]_{1}^{2}$

Evaluate the limits:

$W = a \left( -\dfrac{1}{2} - \left(-\dfrac{1}{1}\right) \right) = a \left( 1 - \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \dfrac{a}{2}$

Equating this to the given work done of $10\text{ J}$:

$\dfrac{a}{2} = 10 \implies a = 20$

The value of the constant $a$ is $20$ in SI units.

Answer: $20$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass $1 \text{ kg}$, initially at rest at the origin, is acted upon by a two-dimensional variable force given by $\vec{F} = (2x \hat{i} + 3y^2 \hat{j}) \text{ N}$, where $x$ and $y$ are in metres. The speed of the particle when it reaches the coordinates $(2 \text{ m}, 2 \text{ m})$ is:
questions.solution:
The work done by a two-dimensional variable force is calculated by integrating the force components along their respective axes.

$W = \int \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = \int (F_x dx + F_y dy)$

Given $\vec{F} = (2x \hat{i} + 3y^2 \hat{j}) \text{ N}$, the work done from $(0,0)$ to $(2,2)$ is:
$W_x = \int_{0}^{2} 2x dx = \left[ x^2 \right]_{0}^{2} = 4 \text{ J}$
$W_y = \int_{0}^{2} 3y^2 dy = \left[ y^3 \right]_{0}^{2} = 8 \text{ J}$

Total work done, $W = W_x + W_y = 4 + 8 = 12 \text{ J}$

According to the work-energy theorem, the total work done is equal to the change in kinetic energy:
$W = \Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2 - \dfrac{1}{2} m u^2$

Since the particle starts from rest ($u = 0$) and its mass $m = 1 \text{ kg}$:
$12 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1 \times v^2$
$v^2 = 24$
$v = \sqrt{24} = 2\sqrt{6} \text{ m/s}$

Answer: $2\sqrt{6} \text{ m/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A car of mass $1200\text{ kg}$ is moving up an inclined plane of angle $30^{\circ}$ with a constant speed of $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$. A constant frictional force of $2000\text{ N}$ opposes the motion of the car. The power delivered by the engine of the car in $\text{kW}$ is : (Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
Since the car moves with a constant speed, its acceleration is zero, which means the net force acting on it is zero.

The engine must provide an upward force along the incline to balance both the component of the car's weight acting down the incline and the opposing frictional force.

Component of weight down the incline $= mg \sin\theta$
$= 1200 \times 10 \times \sin(30^{\circ})$
$= 12000 \times 0.5 = 6000\text{ N}$

Total force required by the engine, $F_{\text{engine}} = mg \sin\theta + f$
$F_{\text{engine}} = 6000 + 2000 = 8000\text{ N}$

Power delivered by the engine, $P = F_{\text{engine}} \times v$
$P = 8000 \times 10 = 80000\text{ W}$
$P = 80\text{ kW}$

Answer: $80$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small ball is dropped from a height of $20\text{ m}$ above a horizontal floor. After striking the floor, it rebounds to a maximum height of $5\text{ m}$. The percentage of kinetic energy lost by the ball during the collision with the floor is:
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the ball be $m$.

The kinetic energy of the ball just before striking the floor is equal to its initial potential energy:
$K_{i} = mgh_{i} = mg(20)$

The kinetic energy of the ball just after the rebound is equal to the potential energy at its maximum rebound height:
$K_{f} = mgh_{f} = mg(5)$

The loss in kinetic energy during the collision is:
$\Delta K = K_{i} - K_{f} = 20mg - 5mg = 15mg$

The percentage loss of kinetic energy is:
$\text{Percentage loss} = \left( \dfrac{\Delta K}{K_{i}} \right) \times 100$
$\text{Percentage loss} = \left( \dfrac{15mg}{20mg} \right) \times 100 = 75\%$

Answer: $75\%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An upward force acting on a body varies with its vertical displacement $y$. The force increases linearly from $0$ to $400$ N as the displacement increases from $y = 0$ to $y = 10$ m. If the total time taken for this displacement is $4$ s, the average power delivered by the force is :
questions.solution:
Work done by the force is given by the area under the Force-displacement graph.

Since the force increases linearly from $0$ to $400$ N over a displacement of $10$ m, the area represents a triangle.

$W = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$

$W = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 400 = 2000$ J.

Average power is the total work done divided by the total time taken.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The instantaneous power delivered by the centripetal force to a particle in uniform circular motion is always zero.

Reason (R): The magnitude of centripetal force acting on a particle of mass $m$ moving with speed $v$ in a circle of radius $r$ is $\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
The instantaneous power is given by the dot product of force and velocity vectors: $P = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v} = Fv \cos \theta$.

In uniform circular motion, the centripetal force is directed radially inward towards the centre, while the velocity vector is tangential to the circular path. Thus, the angle $\theta$ between them is $90^\circ$.

Therefore, $P = Fv \cos 90^\circ = 0$. Hence, Assertion (A) is true.

The magnitude of centripetal force is indeed given by the formula $\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. Hence, Reason (R) is also true.

However, the formula for the magnitude of the force does not explain why the power is zero; the correct explanation is the perpendicularity of the force and velocity vectors. Thus, (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

Answer: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle moving along the $x$-axis is subjected to a variable force $F = c x^n$, where $c$ and $n$ are constants. It is observed that the work done by this force in displacing the particle from the origin ($x = 0$) to a position $x_0$ is directly proportional to $x_0^3$. How does the force $F$ depend on the position $x$?
questions.solution:
The work done by a variable force is calculated by integrating the force over the displacement.

$W = \int_{0}^{x_0} F \, dx$

Substitute the given force expression $F = c x^n$:

$W = \int_{0}^{x_0} c x^n \, dx$

Applying the power rule for integration:

$W = c \left[ \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} \right]_{0}^{x_0} = \dfrac{c}{n+1} x_0^{n+1}$

This shows that the work done $W$ is proportional to $x_0^{n+1}$.

The problem states that $W \propto x_0^3$. By comparing the exponents, we get:

$n + 1 = 3 \implies n = 2$

Substituting $n = 2$ back into the force equation gives $F = c x^2$.

Therefore, the force is directly proportional to the square of the position, $F \propto x^2$.

Answer: $F \propto x^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass $m$ moving along the positive $x$-axis experiences a position-dependent retarding force $F = -k\sqrt{x}$, where $k$ is a positive constant. If the particle enters the region at $x=0$ with a velocity $v_0$ and comes to rest at $x=x_0$, the value of the constant $k$ is :
questions.solution:
The work done by the retarding force as the particle moves from $x=0$ to $x=x_0$ is given by:

$W = \int_{0}^{x_0} F dx = \int_{0}^{x_0} (-k\sqrt{x}) dx$

$W = -k \left[ \dfrac{x^{3/2}}{3/2} \right]_{0}^{x_0} = -\dfrac{2}{3} k x_0^{3/2}$

According to the work-energy theorem, the net work done is equal to the change in kinetic energy:

$W = K_f - K_i$

$-\dfrac{2}{3} k x_0^{3/2} = 0 - \dfrac{1}{2} m v_0^2$

Solving for $k$, we get:

$k = \dfrac{3 m v_0^2}{4 x_0^{3/2}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{3 m v_0^2}{4 x_0^{3/2}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
An electric motor operates a pump with an efficiency of $60\%$. The pump lifts $3600$ L of water to a height of $15$ m in $2$ minutes. What is the input power consumed by the electric motor?
(Take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$ and density of water $= 1$ kg/L)
questions.solution:
Given:
Volume of water, $V = 3600$ L
Mass of water, $m = 3600$ kg (since density is $1$ kg/L)
Height, $h = 15$ m
Time, $t = 2$ minutes $= 120$ s
Efficiency, $\eta = 60\% = 0.6$

The useful work done by the pump (output work) is:
$W = mgh = 3600 \times 10 \times 15 = 540000$ J

The output power of the pump is:
$P_{\text{out}} = \dfrac{W}{t} = \dfrac{540000}{120} = 4500$ W $= 4.5$ kW

Efficiency is defined as the ratio of output power to input power:
$\eta = \dfrac{P_{\text{out}}}{P_{\text{in}}}$

Therefore, the input power is:
$P_{\text{in}} = \dfrac{P_{\text{out}}}{\eta} = \dfrac{4.5}{0.6} = 7.5$ kW.

Answer: $7.5$ kW

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An escalator in a shopping mall moves passengers to a floor $10\text{ m}$ above. A steady stream of passengers steps onto the escalator at a rate of $30\text{ passengers per minute}$. If the average mass of a passenger is $60\text{ kg}$ and $20\%$ of the input electrical energy is lost to friction, what is the minimum input electrical power required by the escalator motor? (Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
Average mass flow rate of passengers, $\dfrac{dm}{dt} = \dfrac{30 \times 60}{60} = 30\text{ kg s}^{-1}$

Useful mechanical power output required, $P_{\text{out}} = \left(\dfrac{dm}{dt}\right)gh = 30 \times 10 \times 10 = 3000\text{ W} = 3.0\text{ kW}$

Since $20\%$ of the input energy is lost to friction, the efficiency of the motor is $80\%$.

Input electrical power, $P_{\text{in}} = \dfrac{P_{\text{out}}}{0.80} = \dfrac{3.0}{0.80} = 3.75\text{ kW}$

Answer: $3.75\text{ kW}$

questions.q: A particle moves with a velocity $\vec{v} = (4\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + c\hat{k}) \mathrm{~m~s}^{-1}$ under the influence of a constant force $\vec{F} = (5\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 4\hat{k}) \mathrm{~N}$. If the instantaneous power supplied to the particle is $2 \mathrm{~W}$, the value of the unknown component $c$ is:
questions.solution:
Instantaneous power is given by the dot product of force and velocity vectors:

$P = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v}$

Given $\vec{F} = (5\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 4\hat{k}) \mathrm{~N}$ and $\vec{v} = (4\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + c\hat{k}) \mathrm{~m~s}^{-1}$, we have:

$P = (5)(4) + (3)(-2) + (-4)(c)$

$P = 20 - 6 - 4c = 14 - 4c$

We are given that the power $P = 2 \mathrm{~W}$. Equating the two:

$14 - 4c = 2$

$4c = 12 \implies c = 3$

Answer: $3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $2\text{ kg}$ starts from rest at $x=0$ on a horizontal surface. It is pulled by a constant external force of $20\text{ N}$ in the positive $x$-direction. The frictional force $f$ acting on the block varies with position $x$ such that it decreases linearly from $20\text{ N}$ at $x=0$ to $0\text{ N}$ at $x=4\text{ m}$. The kinetic energy of the block at $x=4\text{ m}$ is :
questions.solution:
The work done by the constant external force is:

$W_{\text{ext}} = F \times d = 20 \times 4 = 80\text{ J}$

The frictional force decreases linearly with position. The work done by friction is the negative of the area under the force-position graph (which forms a right-angled triangle):

$W_{\text{friction}} = - \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} \right)$

$W_{\text{friction}} = - \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 20 \right) = -40\text{ J}$

The net work done on the block is:

$W_{\text{net}} = W_{\text{ext}} + W_{\text{friction}} = 80 - 40 = 40\text{ J}$

By the work-energy theorem, the net work done is equal to the change in kinetic energy:

$W_{\text{net}} = K_f - K_i$

Since the block starts from rest, $K_i = 0$. Therefore, the final kinetic energy is:

$K_f = 40\text{ J}$

Answer: $40\text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A water pump has a power rating of $2$ kW. How much time will it take to lift $500$ kg of water to an overhead tank situated at a height of $20$ m?
(Take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$)
questions.solution:
Given:
Power of the pump, $P = 2$ kW $= 2000$ W
Mass of water, $m = 500$ kg
Height, $h = 20$ m
Acceleration due to gravity, $g = 10$ m/s$^2$

The work done against gravity is:
$W = mgh = 500 \times 10 \times 20 = 100000$ J

Power is the rate of doing work, $P = \dfrac{W}{t}$.
Rearranging for time $t$:
$t = \dfrac{W}{P} = \dfrac{100000}{2000} = 50$ s.

Answer: $50$ s

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An object with an initial kinetic energy of $20 \text{ J}$ is subjected to a constant force $\vec{F} = (4 \hat{i} - 3 \hat{j}) \text{ N}$. Under the influence of this force, the object undergoes a displacement $\Delta \vec{r} = (6 \hat{i} + 8 \hat{j}) \text{ m}$. The kinetic energy of the object at the end of this displacement is
questions.solution:
According to the work-energy theorem, the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: $W = K_f - K_i$.

The work done by the constant force is given by the dot product of the force and displacement vectors:
$W = \vec{F} \cdot \Delta \vec{r} = (4 \hat{i} - 3 \hat{j}) \cdot (6 \hat{i} + 8 \hat{j})$
$W = (4)(6) + (-3)(8) = 24 - 24 = 0 \text{ J}$

Since the force and displacement vectors are orthogonal, the work done is zero.

Using the work-energy theorem:
$0 = K_f - 20$
$K_f = 20 \text{ J}$

The kinetic energy of the object remains unchanged.

Answer: 20 J

questions.q: An object with an initial kinetic energy of $15\text{ J}$ is acted upon simultaneously by two constant forces $\vec{F}_1 = (2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - \hat{k})\text{ N}$ and $\vec{F}_2 = (4\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k})\text{ N}$. Under the influence of these forces, the object moves from an initial point $A(1, 2, -1)\text{ m}$ to a final point $B(3, 4, 2)\text{ m}$. The final kinetic energy of the object is
questions.solution:
First, find the net force acting on the object by adding the individual forces:
$\vec{F}_{net} = \vec{F}_1 + \vec{F}_2$
$\vec{F}_{net} = (2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - \hat{k}) + (4\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}) = (6\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k})\text{ N}$

Next, determine the displacement vector by subtracting the initial position coordinates from the final position coordinates:
$\Delta\vec{r} = \vec{r}_B - \vec{r}_A$
$\Delta\vec{r} = (3 - 1)\hat{i} + (4 - 2)\hat{j} + (2 - (-1))\hat{k} = (2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k})\text{ m}$

Calculate the net work done using the dot product of net force and displacement:
$W = \vec{F}_{net} \cdot \Delta\vec{r}$
$W = (6)(2) + (2)(2) + (1)(3) = 12 + 4 + 3 = 19\text{ J}$

Finally, apply the work-energy theorem to find the final kinetic energy:
$W = K_f - K_i$
$19 = K_f - 15$
$K_f = 15 + 19 = 34\text{ J}$

Answer: $34\text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A simple pendulum has a string of length $2\text{ m}$ and a bob of mass $m$. The bob is released from rest when the string is horizontal. At the lowest point of its path, the bob strikes a stationary heavy block and loses $50\%$ of its kinetic energy in the collision. The maximum angle the string makes with the vertical during the subsequent rebound is:
questions.solution:
Let the length of the pendulum be $L = 2\text{ m}$.

When released from the horizontal position, the initial height of the bob relative to the lowest point is $h_{1} = L$.
By conservation of mechanical energy, the kinetic energy of the bob just before impact at the lowest point is:
$K_{1} = mgL$

During the collision, the bob loses $50\%$ of its kinetic energy. The kinetic energy remaining just after the collision is:
$K_{2} = K_{1} - 0.5K_{1} = 0.5K_{1} = 0.5mgL$

Let $h_{2}$ be the maximum height reached by the bob during the rebound. Equating the remaining kinetic energy to the potential energy at this height:
$mgh_{2} = 0.5mgL$
$h_{2} = 0.5L$

From the geometry of a simple pendulum, the height $h$ reached when the string makes an angle $\theta$ with the vertical is given by $h = L(1 - \cos\theta)$.

Substituting $h_{2} = 0.5L$ into the geometric relation:
$0.5L = L(1 - \cos\theta)$
$0.5 = 1 - \cos\theta$
$\cos\theta = 0.5$

Therefore, the maximum angle is $\theta = 60^{\circ}$.

Answer: $60^{\circ}$

Let $h_{2}$ be the maximum height reached by the bob during the rebound. Equating the remaining kinetic energy to the potential energy at this height:
$mgh_{2} = 0.5mgL$
$h_{2} = 0.5L$

From the geometry of a simple pendulum, the height $h$ reached when the string makes an angle $\theta$ with the vertical is given by $h = L(1 - \cos\theta)$.

Substituting $h_{2} = 0.5L$ into the geometric relation:
$0.5L = L(1 - \cos\theta)$
$0.5 = 1 - \cos\theta$
$\cos\theta = 0.5$

Therefore, the maximum angle is $\theta = 60^{\circ}$.

Answer: $60^{\circ}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass $2 \text{ kg}$ moves along the x-axis. Its position varies with time according to the equation $x = t^3 + t$, where $x$ is in metres and $t$ is in seconds. The instantaneous power delivered to the particle by the net force at $t = 2 \text{ s}$ is:
questions.solution:
Given, position of the particle is $x = t^3 + t$

Velocity of the particle is:
$v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt}(t^3 + t) = 3t^2 + 1$

Acceleration of the particle is:
$a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt}(3t^2 + 1) = 6t$

At $t = 2 \text{ s}$:
$v = 3(2)^2 + 1 = 13 \text{ m s}^{-1}$
$a = 6(2) = 12 \text{ m s}^{-2}$

According to Newton's second law, the net force acting on the particle is:
$F = ma = 2 \times 12 = 24 \text{ N}$

The instantaneous power delivered by the net force is:
$P = Fv = 24 \times 13 = 312 \text{ W}$

Answer: $312 \text{ W}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II regarding a ball striking the ground and rebounding. List-I contains the percentage of kinetic energy lost during the collision, and List-II contains the corresponding ratio of the rebound velocity to the impact velocity ($v_f / v_i$).

List-I (Percentage of KE lost)List-II (Ratio $v_f / v_i$)
(A) $36\%$(I) $0.5$
(B) $51\%$(II) $0$
(C) $75\%$(III) $0.8$
(D) $100\%$(IV) $0.7$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Let initial kinetic energy be $K_i$ and final kinetic energy be $K_f$.

Since $K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, the velocity ratio is $\dfrac{v_f}{v_i} = \sqrt{\dfrac{K_f}{K_i}}$.

If $36\%$ of kinetic energy is lost, $64\%$ is retained. $\dfrac{K_f}{K_i} = 0.64 \Rightarrow \dfrac{v_f}{v_i} = \sqrt{0.64} = 0.8$. (A) matches (III).

If $51\%$ of kinetic energy is lost, $49\%$ is retained. $\dfrac{K_f}{K_i} = 0.49 \Rightarrow \dfrac{v_f}{v_i} = \sqrt{0.49} = 0.7$. (B) matches (IV).

If $75\%$ of kinetic energy is lost, $25\%$ is retained. $\dfrac{K_f}{K_i} = 0.25 \Rightarrow \dfrac{v_f}{v_i} = \sqrt{0.25} = 0.5$. (C) matches (I).

If $100\%$ of kinetic energy is lost, $0\%$ is retained. $\dfrac{K_f}{K_i} = 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{v_f}{v_i} = 0$. (D) matches (II).

Answer: (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An object of mass $2 \text{ kg}$, initially at rest, moves along the x-axis under the action of a variable force. The force-position ($F-x$) graph consists of a triangular region from $x = 0$ to $x = 4 \text{ m}$ where the force increases linearly from zero to a maximum value $F_0$ at $x = 2 \text{ m}$ and then decreases linearly to zero at $x = 4 \text{ m}$. This is followed by a rectangular region from $x = 4 \text{ m}$ to $x = 6 \text{ m}$ where the force is constant at $-\dfrac{F_0}{2}$. If the speed of the object at $x = 6 \text{ m}$ is $4 \text{ m/s}$, the value of $F_0$ is:
questions.solution:
According to the work-energy theorem, the net work done by the force equals the change in kinetic energy of the object.

The work done is the area under the $F-x$ graph.
Area of the triangular region (from $x = 0$ to $x = 4 \text{ m}$) = $\dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times F_0 = 2F_0$
Area of the rectangular region (from $x = 4 \text{ m}$ to $x = 6 \text{ m}$) = $\text{width} \times \text{height} = 2 \times \left(-\dfrac{F_0}{2}\right) = -F_0$

Net work done $W = 2F_0 - F_0 = F_0$

Change in kinetic energy $\Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - 0 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times (4)^2 = 16 \text{ J}$

Equating work done to the change in kinetic energy:
$F_0 = 16 \text{ N}$

Answer: $16 \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $1 \text{ kg}$ is initially at rest on a rough horizontal surface having a coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu_k = 0.4$. It is pushed along the surface by a variable horizontal force. The applied force decreases linearly with position $x$ from $10 \text{ N}$ at $x = 0$ to $0 \text{ N}$ at $x = 10 \text{ m}$. The maximum kinetic energy attained by the block during its motion is: (Take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.solution:
The kinetic friction acting on the block is $f_k = \mu_k mg = 0.4 \times 1 \times 10 = 4 \text{ N}$.

The applied force is $F(x) = 10 - x$.
The net force on the block is $F_{\text{net}} = F(x) - f_k = 10 - x - 4 = 6 - x$.

The kinetic energy of the block will be maximum when its acceleration becomes zero, which occurs when the net force is zero.
$F_{\text{net}} = 0 \Rightarrow 6 - x = 0 \Rightarrow x = 6 \text{ m}$.

The maximum kinetic energy is equal to the net work done on the block up to $x = 6 \text{ m}$.
$W_{\text{net}} = \int_{0}^{6} F_{\text{net}} \, dx = \int_{0}^{6} (6 - x) \, dx$
$W_{\text{net}} = \left[ 6x - \dfrac{x^2}{2} \right]_{0}^{6} = \left( 36 - \dfrac{36}{2} \right) = 18 \text{ J}$.

Thus, the maximum kinetic energy attained is $18 \text{ J}$.

Answer: $18 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electric pump is used to fill an overhead tank situated at a height of $15\text{ m}$. The volume of water pumped varies linearly with time, such that the graph of volume in litres ($y$-axis) versus time in seconds ($x$-axis) is a straight line passing through the origin and the point $(50\text{ s}, 400\text{ L})$. If the overall efficiency of the pump is $80\%$, what is the electrical power consumed by the pump? (Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$ and density of water $= 10^3\text{ kg m}^{-3}$)
questions.solution:
Slope of the volume-time graph gives the volume flow rate:
$\dfrac{dV}{dt} = \dfrac{400 - 0}{50 - 0} = 8\text{ L s}^{-1} = 8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3\text{ s}^{-1}$

Mass flow rate of water, $\dfrac{dm}{dt} = \dfrac{dV}{dt} \times \rho = 8 \times 10^{-3} \times 10^3 = 8\text{ kg s}^{-1}$

Useful mechanical power delivered to the water:
$P_{\text{out}} = \left(\dfrac{dm}{dt}\right)gh = 8 \times 10 \times 15 = 1200\text{ W} = 1.2\text{ kW}$

Since the efficiency of the pump is $80\%$, the electrical power consumed (input power) is:
$P_{\text{in}} = \dfrac{P_{\text{out}}}{0.80} = \dfrac{1.2}{0.80} = 1.5\text{ kW}$

Answer: $1.50\text{ kW}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electric pump has an input power rating of $5\text{ kW}$ and operates with an efficiency of $80\%$. It is used to lift water from a well of depth $20\text{ m}$. What is the volume of water lifted by the pump per minute? (Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$ and density of water $= 1000\text{ kg m}^{-3}$)
questions.solution:
Input power of the pump, $P_{\text{in}} = 5\text{ kW} = 5000\text{ W}$

Useful output power, $P_{\text{out}} = P_{\text{in}} \times \text{efficiency} = 5000 \times \dfrac{80}{100} = 4000\text{ W}$

Let the mass of water lifted per second be $\dfrac{dm}{dt}$.

Power used in lifting water, $P_{\text{out}} = \dfrac{dm}{dt} g h$

$4000 = \dfrac{dm}{dt} \times 10 \times 20$

$\dfrac{dm}{dt} = \dfrac{4000}{200} = 20\text{ kg s}^{-1}$

Mass of water lifted in one minute $= 20 \times 60 = 1200\text{ kg}$

Since the density of water is $1000\text{ kg m}^{-3}$ (which is equivalent to $1\text{ kg L}^{-1}$), the volume of water lifted per minute is $1200\text{ L}$.

Answer: $1200\text{ L}$

questions.q: A car of mass $1000\text{ kg}$ accelerates uniformly from rest to a velocity of $20\text{ m/s}$ in $10\text{ s}$. The average power delivered by the engine during this time interval is
questions.solution:
According to the work-energy theorem, the total work done by the engine equals the change in kinetic energy of the car.

Initial kinetic energy, $K_i = 0$

Final kinetic energy, $K_f = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1000 \times (20)^2 = 200000\text{ J}$

Work done, $W = \Delta K = 200000\text{ J}$

Average power is the total work done divided by the total time taken:

$P_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{W}{t} = \dfrac{200000\text{ J}}{10\text{ s}} = 20000\text{ W}$

$P_{\text{avg}} = 20\text{ kW}$

Answer: $20\text{ kW}$

$a=\frac{F}{m_1+m_2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle is thrown vertically upwards with velocity $11.2 \mathrm{~km} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ from the surface of earth. Calculate its velocity at height $3 R$. Where $R$ is the radius of earth.
questions.solution:
Let a particle of mass $m$ is thrown vertically upward with velocity $v$. Let its velocity be $v^{\prime}$ at a height $3 R$ from the surface of the earth. According to the conservation of energy,
$\frac{1}{2} m v^2-\frac{G M m}{R}=\frac{1}{2} m v^{\prime 2}-\frac{G M m}{(R+3 R)}$
$v^2-\frac{2 G M}{R}=v^{\prime 2}-\frac{2 G M}{4 R}$
$v^2-v^{\prime 2}=\frac{-2 G M}{4 R}+\frac{2 G M}{R}=\frac{6}{4} \frac{G M}{R}$
$v^{\prime 2}=v^2-\frac{6}{4} \frac{G M}{R}$
$v^{\prime 2}=\sqrt{(11.2)^2-\frac{3}{2} g R} \quad\left(\because g=\frac{G M}{R^2}\right)$
$=\sqrt{(11.2)^2-\frac{3}{2} \times \frac{9.8 \times 6400}{1000}}$
$=\sqrt{(11.2)^2-(94.08)}$
$=5.6 \mathrm{~km} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$

$v^2-\frac{2 G M}{R}=v^{\prime 2}-\frac{2 G M}{4 R}$

$v^{\prime 2}=v^2-\frac{6}{4} \frac{G M}{R}$

$=5.6 \mathrm{~km} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$

questions.solution:
According to work energy theorem,

$\begin{aligned}$& W=$\Delta \mathrm{K} \cdot \mathrm{E} . \quad \Rightarrow$W=$\frac{1}{2}$m v_2^2-$\frac{1}{2}$m v_1^2 \\
\Rightarrow & F $\cdot$d x=$\mathrm{K} \cdot \mathrm{E} \cdot$f-$\frac{1}{2} \times$10 $\times$100 \\
\Rightarrow & F $\cdot$d x=$\mathrm{K} \cdot \mathrm{E} \cdot$f-500 \\
\Rightarrow & \int_{20}^{30}-0.1 x d x=$\mathrm{K} \cdot \mathrm{E} \cdot$f-500 \\
\Rightarrow & -0.1$\left[\frac{x^2}{2}\right]_{20}^{30}=\mathrm{K} \cdot \mathrm{E} \cdot$f-500 \\
\Rightarrow & -0.1$\left[\frac{900-400}{2}\right]=\mathrm{K} \cdot \mathrm{E} \cdot$f-500
\end{aligned}

\Rightarrow $\mathrm{K}_{\cdot} \mathrm{E}_{\cdot f}=$500-25=475 $\mathrm{~J}$

questions.q: A particle of mass 7 kg is executing circular motion with time period of 11 sec . Find out centripetal force, if radius of circle is 10 m .
questions.solution:
Given, Time period $(\mathrm{T})=11 \mathrm{sec}$, mass of particle $(\mathrm{m})=7 \mathrm{~kg}$
and $\quad$ radius $(\mathrm{r})=10 \mathrm{~m}$
$\therefore \quad$ Speed of particle, $v=\frac{2 \pi r}{T}=\frac{2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 10}{11}$ $=\frac{40}{7} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$
$\therefore$ Centripetal force, $\mathrm{F}=\frac{\mathrm{mv}^2}{\mathrm{r}}=\frac{7 \times \frac{40}{7} \times \frac{40}{7}}{10}=\frac{160}{7} \mathrm{~N}$

questions.q: Kinetic energy of a particle is increased by 4 times. What will be the relation between initial and final momentum?
questions.solution:
$\because$ Relation between kinetic energy and momentum is $\mathrm{p}_1=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mk}_1}$
$\because$ Kinetic energy is increased by 4 times
$\therefore \quad \mathrm{k}_2=4 \mathrm{k}_1$
Hence, $\mathrm{p}_2=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mk}_2}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{~m}\left(4 \mathrm{k}_1\right)}=2 \sqrt{2 \mathrm{mk}_1}$
or $\quad \mathrm{p}_2=2 \mathrm{p}_1$

questions.q: A uniform rod of length $l$ is free to rotate in a vertical plane about a fixed horizontal axis through $B$. The rod begins rotating from rest from its unstable equilibrium position. When, it has turned through an angle $\theta$, its angular velocity $\omega$ is given by
questions.solution:
When the rod rotates through an angle $\theta$, the centre of gravity falls through a distance h. From $\triangle B C G^{\prime} \begin{aligned} & \cos \theta=\frac{(l / 2)-h}{\mu_2} \\ & or, h=\frac{1}{2}(1-\cos \theta)\end{aligned}$

From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get
$\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{m l^2}{3}\right) \omega^2 & =m g \frac{1}{2}(1-\cos \theta) \\ \omega & =\sqrt{\frac{6 g}{l}} \sin \frac{\theta}{2}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two blocks of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ are connected by a spring of spring constant $k$. The block of mass $m_2$ is given a sharp empulse so that it acquires a velocity $v_0$ towards right. Find the maximum elongation that the spring will suffer.
questions.solution:
The velocity of centre of mass
$v_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{m_1 v_1+m_2 v_2}{m_1+m_2}$
When $v_1=0$ and $v_2=v_0$, then
$v_{c m}=\frac{m_2 v_0}{m_1+m_2}$
Now, let $x$ be the elongation in the spring.
Change in potential energy $=$ potential energy stored in spring
$\begin{gathered}
\Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{2} m_2 v_0^2-\frac{1}{2}\left(m_1+m_2\right) \\
\left(\frac{m_2 V_0}{m_1+m_2}\right)^2=\frac{1}{2} k x^2
\end{gathered}$
This gives, $x=\left(\frac{m_1 m_2}{m_1+m_2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} v_0$

questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & p^2=2 M E \\ & \therefore \quad p \propto \sqrt{E} \\ & \therefore \quad \frac{p_1}{p_2}=\sqrt{\frac{E_1}{E_2}}=\sqrt{\frac{E}{E+3 E}}=\frac{1}{2} \\ & \end{aligned} \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad p_2 & =2 p_1 \\ \% \text{ Increase } & =\frac{p_2-p_1}{p_1} \times 100\end{aligned} \Rightarrow \frac{2 p_1-p_1}{p_1} \times 100=100 \%$
